full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm downgrading the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. What you observed is the textbook Nowak–May spatial Prisoner's Dilemma at low temptation. That game settles into a frozen or periodic pattern, and rare random flips occasionally kick it back into short bursts of change. The "domain coarsening" label is probably wrong: these features fit a system relaxing into a frozen pattern, not domains that keep growing.

**1. The core rule is exactly the Nowak–May model.** In that model players on a square lattice play the game with all their neighbours, add up the payoffs, and then each player imitates the strategy of those neighboring players (including herself) who has scored the highest payoff. Due to the deterministic, simultaneous update this evolutionary rule defines a cellular automaton. Your payoffs (R=1, P=S=0, T=b) are their standard rescaled matrix. With S=0 this is called the "weak" dilemma, but when played as a spatial game the weak version has the same qualitative properties as the typical version with c<0. That covers the (1.5, −0.5) members of the class too. The "8 neighbours plus yourself" setup is also theirs: every player plays also with herself, i.e., it is an 8+1 neighborhood.

**2. Why activity dies away (negative trend).** A scan of the deterministic Moore-neighbourhood game found chaos only for 1.8 < T ≤ 2 … whereas for the other regions only a few periodic states are present. The same study says the system only changes behaviour at some thresholds by the nature of the game rules, and not continuously. That explains why runs at T=1.3 and T=1.5 fall in the same class. Both are below the chaotic threshold, so after the opening shake-out the grid freezes or cycles, and activity drops.

**3. Why activity is bursty (high CV).** The majority-vote or swap events happen with probability 0.001–0.005, so the frozen pattern is only rarely disturbed. Each disturbance sets off a brief local cascade before the grid freezes again. That is the predictable result of a nearly frozen deterministic system plus sparse noise. Adding small random perturbations to Nowak–May is itself a documented extension: proposed by Mukherji et al. (1996): After following the Nowak and May update rule, each cooperator has a small independent probability, ϕ, of cheating by switching to defection. I only saw that extension described in a textbook exercise, not their actual results. Mixing payoff-copying with conformity is also an established line of work: some works have considered the mixed rule in combination with the payoff-driven and conformity-driven strategy update procedures. One example is Szolnoki & Perc, J. R. Soc. Interface 2015.

**4. Why I'm calling the coarsening label an artifact.** Many domains with a correlation length of about 2 means lots of small clusters, not large domains merging over time. The negative activity trend most likely passed the coarsening test because the boundaries stop moving once the grid freezes, not because domains grow. Getting the same behaviour across 25 rule programs, both update types and both payoff settings also points to the generic frozen low-temptation regime rather than anything specific to this exact rule combination.

**What is still unconfirmed:** I found no paper on this exact hybrid (simultaneous imitate-the-best plus rare majority sweeps) or one that measures its burst statistics. But by your own criterion, an undocumented rule combination is not a discovery. I found nothing to suggest the bursts are anything other than noise-triggered relaxation. They would only count as new if they showed heavy-tailed, scale-free avalanche sizes, which these summary features can't show.
